title: Area I review: Preflight Preparation
intro: These questions mix all eight Tasks of Area I, from pilot qualifications to human factors. Many of them join two Tasks in one real preflight situation, just like the checkride.

questions.q: Your route passes over a town. The highest obstacle within 2,000 feet of your path is a water tower 350 feet tall. The ground there is 900 feet MSL. What is the lowest altitude you may fly over the town?
options: 1,400 ft MSL
1,750 ft MSL
2,250 ft MSL
1,900 ft MSL
questions.why: Over a congested area you must stay 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft horizontally [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]]. The tower top is 900 + 350 = 1,250 ft MSL, so the minimum is 1,250 + 1,000 = 2,250 ft MSL.

questions.q: Your last drink was at 2000. At 0700 the next morning, 11 hours later, a breath test would show an alcohol level of 0.05. May you fly as PIC?
options: Yes. More than 8 hours have passed.
No. Your alcohol level must also be below 0.04.
Yes, as long as you feel fine and have no hangover.
Yes, but only solo with no passengers.
questions.why: Both limits apply: 8 hours since the last drink AND an alcohol level below 0.04 [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17(a)]]. A pilot at 0.04 or more after 8 hours cannot fly until it drops below that [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

questions.q: Your airplane's transponder was last tested and inspected in September 2024. Today is October 16, 2026, and you plan to land at an airport inside Class C airspace. What is true?
options: It is fine. Transponder tests are only required for flights operated under instrument flight rules.
It is fine. The test stays valid for 36 calendar months, which runs through the end of September 2027.
It is fine as long as ADS-B Out works, since ADS-B Out replaces the transponder in Class C airspace.
Not legal. The test expired at the end of September 2026, and Class C also needs a transponder and ADS-B Out.
questions.why: A transponder may not be used unless it was tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]], so a September 2024 test lasted through September 30, 2026. Unless ATC authorizes otherwise, Class C requires the equipment in 91.215 and 91.225 [[60:455|14 CFR 91.130(d)]]: a transponder with altitude reporting [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)]] and ADS-B Out [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)]]. ADS-B Out does not replace the transponder.

questions.q: Your ETA is 2100Z. The destination TAF includes 'TEMPO 1620/1623 3SM SHRA BKN020'. What does this group tell you?
options: From 2000Z on, a whole new forecast of 3 SM in rain showers with a 2,000 ft broken ceiling replaces the earlier one
Brief spells of 3 SM in rain showers under a 2,000 ft broken ceiling, each 1 hour or less and totaling under half of 2000Z to 2300Z
There is a 30 percent chance of rain showers with 3 SM visibility and a 2,000 ft broken ceiling between 2000Z and 2300Z
Rain showers with 3 SM visibility and a 2,000 ft broken ceiling were observed at the airport at 2000Z
questions.why: TEMPO means temporary changes with more than a 50 percent chance, each lasting 1 hour or less, adding up to less than half of the period given [[28:417|AWH 27-16]]. FM starts a whole new forecast and PROB30 is a 30 percent chance [[28:416|AWH 27-15]] [[28:418|AWH 27-17]].

questions.q: Four METARs from the same airport on different days are shown below. Which one means the worst takeoff performance for your airplane?
questions.why: High temperature, low pressure and high humidity all raise density altitude, and the airplane performs worse [[1:260|PHAK 11-4]] [[1:261|PHAK 11-5]]. 34/24 is hot with a high dew point (moist air), and A2984 is the lowest pressure. In a METAR the first number is temperature and the second is dew point, in °C [[28:302|AWH 24-18]].

questions.q: You got a third-class medical in March 2023, when you were 39 years old. You turned 40 that June. You fly only as a private pilot. Through what date is the medical good?
options: March 31, 2027
March 31, 2025
March 31, 2028
questions.why: What counts is your age on the date of the exam [[60:208|14 CFR 61.23(d)]]. Under 40, a third-class medical is good for private privileges until the end of the 60th month after the exam month [[60:209|14 CFR 61.23(d)(3)(i)]]. March 2023 plus 60 months is March 2028.

questions.q: In cruise on a cool, humid day (METAR 12/10), your fixed-pitch airplane slowly loses RPM. You pull full carburetor heat. The RPM drops a bit more and the engine runs rough, then the RPM slowly rises. What does this mean?
options: There was no ice, so the rough running is a fault; turn the carb heat off right away
The carb heat is making it worse, so go back to using only partial heat for the rest of the flight
Ice was present and is melting; keep full carb heat on until it is all gone
The engine is failing, so turn off the carb heat, lean the mixture and plan a precautionary landing
questions.why: With ice present, carb heat gives a drop in RPM, then a slow rise as the ice melts; the engine may run rough as melted ice goes through it [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. Leave full heat on until you are sure all the ice is gone. Partial heat can make icing worse [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

questions.q: It is mid-morning. The METAR for your Class D home airport reads: 00000KT 1/2SM FG VV002. You are a private pilot with no instrument rating. Can you depart?
options: Yes, under special VFR with a tower clearance, if you stay clear of clouds
Yes, under basic VFR, because the wind is calm and the fog should lift soon
No. Even special VFR needs at least 1 SM ground visibility to take off.
Yes, if the tower clears you and you stay below 200 feet the whole way
questions.why: Basic VFR in a surface area needs 3 SM ground visibility and a ceiling of at least 1,000 ft [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c)-(d)]]. Special VFR is the fallback, but no one may take off under special VFR unless ground visibility is at least 1 SM [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(c)]]. Here it is 1/2 SM in fog.

questions.q: At night you fly to an unfamiliar airport. Its runway is much narrower than the one you are used to, and light rain is on the windscreen. What error should you guard against?
options: Flying a low approach, because both make you feel higher than you are
Landing long, because rain makes the runway look closer than it really is
Flying a high approach, because both make you feel lower than you are
None, because these illusions only happen in daylight with a clear horizon
questions.why: A narrower-than-usual runway and rain on the windscreen both make you feel higher than you are, so pilots tend to fly a lower approach [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]. Check the Chart Supplement for the runway, and use VASI or PAPI if the airport has one [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].

questions.q: You own your airplane and hold a private pilot certificate. As routine upkeep, you clean the spark plugs, set the gaps, and sign the logbook entry. What does your signature approve?
options: The engine for another 100 hours of flight
The whole airplane as airworthy until its next annual inspection
Nothing yet, because an A&P mechanic must countersign the entry
Return to service for only the spark plug work you did
questions.why: Cleaning spark plugs and setting the gap is preventive maintenance [[60:142|14 CFR Part 43 App. A(c)(20)]], which a pilot may do on an aircraft he or she owns [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]]. A private pilot may approve it for return to service [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]]. The logbook entry needs a description, the date, and your signature, certificate number and kind of certificate, and that signature approves only the work performed [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]].

questions.q: You pass checkpoint A at 1412Z and checkpoint B, 21 NM farther, at 1426Z. Your destination is 42 NM past checkpoint B. At this groundspeed, what is your ETA?
questions.why: Groundspeed = distance ÷ time: 21 NM in 14 minutes is 90 knots [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]]. Time = 42 NM ÷ 90 kt = 0.47 hr, about 28 minutes. 1426Z + 28 minutes = 1454Z.

questions.q: Your briefing includes an AIRMET Zulu along your route. Your trainer has pitot heat but no other ice protection. What is the AIRMET warning about, and what does it mean for you?
options: Moderate turbulence and strong surface winds; slow to maneuvering speed and continue on your route
Moderate icing and freezing levels; your trainer is not certificated for icing, so stay out
IFR conditions and mountain obscuration; stay below the clouds and keep the terrain in sight
Moderate icing; your pitot heat makes the trainer safe to fly in it for short periods
questions.why: AIRMET Zulu covers moderate icing and freezing levels [[28:383|AWH 26-16]]. Flight into known icing is prohibited for aircraft not certificated and equipped for it [[37:15|AC 91-92 para 8.2]], and noncertificated aircraft must exit icing conditions immediately [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]]. Tango is turbulence; Sierra is IFR and obscuration.

questions.q: Today is October 16, 2026. Your last flight review was in May 2024. Last week you made 5 takeoffs and full-stop landings in the same make and model. Friends ask for a ride today. Can you act as PIC?
options: Yes. Your recent landings keep you current to carry passengers.
Yes. The flight review is good until May 2027.
No. The flight review ran out at the end of May 2026.
Yes, as long as you fly only in daylight.
questions.why: To act as PIC you need a flight review since the beginning of the 24th calendar month before this month [[60:237|14 CFR 61.56(c)]]. A May 2024 review lasted through May 31, 2026. The 3 takeoffs and landings in 90 days are a separate rule for passengers and do not replace it [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)]].

questions.q: Your loading: empty airplane 1,450 lb at arm 39.0 in; front seats 320 lb at 37.0 in; 40 gallons of fuel at 48.0 in; baggage 120 lb at 95.0 in. The CG limits are 35.0 to 42.0 in. What is the CG, and what should you do?
options: 40.3 in, within limits: go as loaded with no changes needed
42.9 in, within limits: go as loaded, since 42.9 is inside the range
42.9 in, too far forward: move the baggage farther aft to correct it
42.9 in, too far aft: move baggage forward or leave some behind
questions.why: Fuel weighs 6 lb/gal, so 40 gal = 240 lb [[1:249|PHAK 10-5]]. Moments: 56,550 + 11,840 + 11,520 + 11,400 = 91,310 lb-in. Weight: 1,450 + 320 + 240 + 120 = 2,130 lb. CG = moment ÷ weight = 42.9 in [[1:251|PHAK 10-7]]. That is aft of 42.0, so shift baggage or passengers forward [[22:17|W&B 1-3]].

questions.q: In haze with no clear horizon, the attitude indicator slowly shows a left bank. The turn coordinator shows wings level, the heading indicator is wandering, and the suction gauge reads 2.0 "Hg. What is the most likely problem?
options: A vacuum failure; the electric turn coordinator still shows bank
An electrical failure; trust the attitude indicator for bank
A blocked pitot tube; switch to the alternate static source
A failed turn coordinator; follow the attitude indicator now
questions.why: Normal suction is usually 4.5 to 5.5 "Hg. When it drops, the vacuum-driven attitude and heading indicators may become unstable and wrong [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]. The turn coordinator is usually electric, so you keep a source of bank information [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]. Without a horizon, trust working instruments, not your body [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

questions.q: You plan to cruise VFR at 10,500 feet MSL in Class E airspace. A pilot report says a cloud layer below you has tops at 9,800 feet. Flight visibility is 8 SM. Is your plan legal?
options: Yes. At this altitude you only need to stay 500 feet above the clouds.
Yes. PIREP cloud heights are given AGL, so you are far above the tops.
Yes. With more than 5 SM flight visibility, cloud distance does not matter at all.
No. You would be only 700 feet above the tops, and you need 1,000 feet.
questions.why: At or above 10,000 ft MSL in Class E, you need 5 SM visibility and 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 1 SM horizontal from clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. PIREP altitudes are MSL [[28:310|AWH 24-26]], so 10,500 - 9,800 = 700 ft is not enough.

questions.q: Over mountains, your unpressurized airplane will spend 50 minutes at 13,500 feet MSL before you descend. Under the oxygen rule, what must you do?
options: Every passenger must be provided with supplemental oxygen for the whole 50 minutes
Nothing, because supplemental oxygen is only required above 14,000 feet MSL
The required crew must use oxygen for the entire time spent at that altitude
The required crew must use oxygen for the time beyond the first 30 minutes
questions.why: From above 12,500 up to 14,000 ft MSL, the required crew must use oxygen for the part of the flight at those altitudes that is more than 30 minutes [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(1)]]. The AIM puts it plainly: crew must use oxygen after 30 minutes at those altitudes, so here for the last 20 minutes [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2a]]. Passengers must be provided oxygen only above 15,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(3)]]. The AIM encourages oxygen above 10,000 ft by day anyway [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2a]].

questions.q: In flight, your cockpit NEXRAD shows an intense storm cell about 15 miles ahead, near your course. The image time stamp says 4 minutes old. What is the best plan?
options: Assume the image is older than shown, and turn early to stay 20 miles from the cell
Continue on course, because 15 miles is plenty of room to stay clear of any intense storm cell
Fly through the gap the display shows between the two cells, since the image is only 4 minutes old
Wait until you can see the storm, then pick a path around it in the last few minutes
questions.why: Data-link NEXRAD shows where the weather was, not where it is, and can be 15-20 minutes older than shown [[28:276|AWH 22-21]]; assume at least 7-8 minutes older than the time stamp [[1:334|PHAK 13-24]]. Use it to avoid storms early, not to pick a path through them, and avoid an intense echo by at least 20 miles [[28:276|AWH 22-21]].

questions.q: A flight school uses its airplane for paid lessons. Its last 100-hour inspection was at 4,120.0 hours. At 4,175.0 hours it got its annual inspection. When is the next 100-hour inspection due?
options: 4,220.0 hours
4,275.0 hours
Not until the next annual
4,230.0 hours
questions.why: An airplane used for flight instruction for hire, when the one giving the instruction provides the airplane, needs an annual or 100-hour inspection within the preceding 100 hours [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. An annual can be substituted for a 100-hour [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]], so the clock restarts at 4,175.0 and the next is due at 4,275.0.

questions.q: You are on an active VFR flight plan. Stronger headwinds than forecast mean you will arrive 40 minutes later than the ETA you filed. What should you do?
options: Nothing; the tower at your destination will update it
Close the flight plan now and fly the rest without one
Squawk 7600 so ATC knows you are late
Report a new ETA to Flight Service
questions.why: If your ETE changes by 30 minutes or more, report a new ETA to the nearest FSS [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]]. If you are not heard from within one-half hour after your ETA, a search starts. Control towers do not automatically close VFR flight plans, since they do not know if you are on one [[33:339|AIM 5-1-14]].

questions.q: You fly under BasicMed in a 6-seat airplane that weighs 3,600 lb, with 4 passengers. Which change to your plan would break the BasicMed rules?
options: Cruising at 180 knots indicated
Adding a fifth passenger
Flying a 5,000-lb airplane with 7 seats
Climbing to 18,500 feet MSL
questions.why: BasicMed allows up to 7 occupants, 12,500 lb max takeoff weight, 6 passengers, no more than 250 knots indicated, and no flight above 18,000 ft MSL [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]]. At 18,500 ft you would also be in Class A, which is IFR only [[60:456|14 CFR 91.135]].

questions.q: Flying solo, your takeoff weight is about 2,000 lb. Today two friends and their bags bring it to about 2,200 lb, 10 percent more. About how does your takeoff distance change?
options: At least 21 percent longer
About 10 percent longer
About 5 percent longer
No change, because lift-off speed stays the same
questions.why: A 10 percent increase in takeoff weight gives about a 5 percent higher takeoff speed, at least 9 percent slower acceleration and at least a 21 percent longer takeoff distance [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]. Check the runway length against that before you go [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].

questions.q: On flight following, approach control gave you a squawk code and said "radar contact." The Class B boundary is just ahead. What do you need before you enter it?
options: Nothing more, because two-way radio contact is enough
Only an operating altitude-reporting transponder
A VFR flight plan that is open with Flight Service
An ATC clearance to enter the Class B airspace
questions.why: Regardless of weather, an ATC clearance is required before operating in Class B [[33:179|AIM 3-2-3]] [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131]]. Two-way radio contact is the entry rule for Class C and D, not Class B [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]] [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]]. The pilot keeps the duty to meet entry rules while getting radar advisories [[33:178|AIM 3-2-1]].

questions.q: At night your ammeter shows a steady discharge and the low-voltage light comes on. You think the alternator has failed. What should you do?
options: Shed non-essential loads and land at the nearest suitable airport
Keep everything on and continue, because the battery will last for hours
Turn the transponder and radios off first, since they are never needed at night
Wait until the battery is nearly dead before you turn anything off
questions.why: The battery may last only minutes; a 40-amp load might drain it in about 10 or 15 minutes. Shed non-essential loads right away and plan to land at the nearest suitable airport [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]. Electric flaps and gear may not work on a weak battery [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

questions.q: A cold front is coming. Your standard briefing is 2 hours old. Your friend, also a pilot, says, "No time to check again. Let's just go right now," and wants to skip any update. Which hazardous attitude is this, and what is its antidote?
options: Macho: "Taking chances is foolish."
Impulsivity: "Not so fast. Think first."
Invulnerability: "It could happen to me."
Resignation: "I'm not helpless. I can make a difference."
questions.why: Impulsivity is the urge to do something, anything, right away; its antidote is "Not so fast. Think first." [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]. Get an abbreviated briefing just before takeoff if your standard briefing is 1 hour or more old or the weather is questionable [[37:14|AC 91-92 para 8.1]].
